contracts.name: UniswapV3Pool
contracts.purpose: A Uniswap V3 concentrated-liquidity AMM pool for one token pair and fee tier. Liquidity providers add liquidity to tick ranges and earn fees, traders swap across ticks, and a built-in oracle records price and liquidity accumulators. The pool also supports flash loans and protocol fee collection.

threats.title: Unauthorized initialization
threats.target: Invariant: The pool cannot be used before initialization (unlocked is false until then)
threats.approach: An attacker could call the initialize function with a zero sqrtPriceX96, bypassing the requirement that it should only be called once by a legitimate actor, potentially allowing them to manipulate the initial state of the pool.

threats.title: Liquidity manipulation
threats.target: Invariant: Per-tick gross liquidity never exceeds maxLiquidityPerTick
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit a bug in the mint function to mint liquidity beyond the maxLiquidityPerTick limit by manipulating the tick ranges or the liquidity parameters, leading to an inconsistent state.

threats.title: Oracle manipulation
threats.target: Invariant: The current tick corresponds to the current sqrtPriceX96
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the increaseObservationCardinalityNext function to manipulate the oracle's observations, leading to incorrect price information being used for swaps and potentially profiting from price discrepancies.

threats.title: Fee collection exploitation
threats.target: Asset: protocolFees (token0/token1 accrued for the protocol)
threats.approach: An attacker could repeatedly call the collectProtocol function to withdraw accrued protocol fees before they are properly accounted for, draining the protocol fees intended for liquidity providers.

threats.title: Flash loan abuse
threats.target: Asset: token0 and token1 balances held by the pool
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the flash loan feature to borrow large amounts of token0 or token1, manipulate the market, and then fail to repay the loan, causing a loss of liquidity in the pool.

threats.title: Reentrancy during collect
threats.target: Invariant: After a mint, swap or flash callback, the pool's token balance must have increased by at least the amount owed (including fees)
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the collect function by re-entering it through the callback mechanism, withdrawing more tokens than they are entitled to before the state is updated.

threats.title: Invalid tick range
threats.target: Invariant: tickLower < tickUpper, and both lie within [MIN_TICK, MAX_TICK]
threats.approach: An attacker could attempt to mint liquidity with invalid tick ranges that do not satisfy the invariant, potentially causing the pool to enter an inconsistent state.

threats.title: Protocol fee manipulation
threats.target: Invariant: Fee growth accumulators only increase (modular arithmetic)
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the setFeeProtocol function to set an excessively high fee, leading to unfair profit distribution and discouraging liquidity providers.

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 3 medium severity issues worth a look.

findings.title: Block Timestamp Dependency
findings.description: Block timestamps can be manipulated by miners within a short range
findings.fix: Avoid using timestamps for critical logic or accept ~15 second variance

findings.title: 5 storage slots serialise this contract
findings.description: Every write to these forces the entrypoints touching them into a queue on Monad: slot0, liquidity, feeGrowthGlobal0X128, feeGrowthGlobal1X128, protocolFees.
findings.fix: Key the state by the caller where the value is theirs, or split a shared counter into stripes that sum back.

findings.title: Give 'slot0' a key
findings.description: 'slot0' is one slot written by increaseObservationCardinalityNext, initialize, mint, collect, burn, swap, flash, setFeeProtocol and collectProtocol, and it blocks 45 entrypoint pairs. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 45 fewer blocked pairs
findings.fix:
mapping(address => Slot0) public slot0;

slot0[msg.sender] = newValue;

findings.title: 16 functions have no gas bound
findings.description: solc could not bound these, so their cost depends on a loop whose length is decided at runtime and a caller can push them past the block gas limit: burn, collect, collectProtocol, factory, fee, flash, increaseObservationCardinalityNext, maxLiquidityPerTick, mint, observe, setFeeProtocol, snapshotCumulativesInside, and 4 more.
findings.fix: Bound the loops, or let callers process a range they choose so the work per transaction is theirs to cap.

findings.title: Gas variance costs real money on Monad
findings.description: Monad debits the sender for the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so anything a wallet pads onto the estimate is spent. solc cannot bound burn(int24,int24,uint128), collect(address,int24,int24,uint128,uint128), collectProtocol(address,uint128,uint128) and 13 more, which is where wallets fall back to a large default limit. Affects monad. Unbounded functions: 16.
findings.fix: Bound the loops, and have your frontend set an explicit gas limit for operations whose cost is fixed rather than letting the wallet estimate and pad.

findings.title: Contract is close to the 24 KB ceiling
findings.description: At 21.3 KB the contract is within 15% of the EIP-170 limit that applies everywhere except Monad. Another feature or two and it stops deploying on Ethereum and the L2s. Affects ethereum, base, arbitrum, polygon, bnb. Headroom before EIP-170: 2.7 KB.
findings.fix: Watch the size, or plan the proxy split now rather than under deadline.

findings.title: State contention will serialise this contract
findings.description: 0 of 9 entrypoints can run concurrently, grade F. 45 of 45 entrypoint pairs always collide, on slot0, liquidity, feeGrowthGlobal0X128. This only converts into throughput on a chain that executes transactions in parallel. Monad does; every other chain in this comparison executes sequentially, so the same layout buys nothing there and costs nothing either. Affects monad. Colliding entrypoint pairs: 45 of 45.
findings.fix: Key hot state by sender or by id instead of writing to one shared slot. The Parallel Profiler lists the exact pairs and the variables behind them.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.description: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next. Affects base, arbitrum. Monad hard finality: 600 ms.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.description: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 0 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract. Affects base, arbitrum. Median calldata: 0 B.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.description: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change. Affects monad.

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

Only state-changing functions are traced. View and pure functions cost nothing to call from outside a transaction.

Only execution and intrinsic gas is modelled. Rollups additionally charge for publishing calldata to Ethereum, which is not included. Measured against the live oracles, that fee is around $0.0001 on Base and $0.00002 on Arbitrum even for a 39 KB deployment, three to four orders of magnitude below the execution cost shown, because EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free.
Ethereum storage cost is measured from the EVM. The Monad figure is that measurement adjusted by the published MIP-8 schedule.

contracts.name: UniswapV3Pool

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 1 medium severity issue worth a look.

contracts.purpose: UniswapV3Pool is a single concentrated-liquidity AMM pool for one token0/token1 pair at a fixed fee tier and tick spacing. It lets liquidity providers add or remove liquidity over tick ranges and lets traders swap or flash-borrow. It also maintains a price oracle and accrues swap fees and protocol fees.

threats.title: Unauthorized initialization
threats.target: Invariant: initialize can run only once
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit a vulnerability in the constructor or the initialization process to call initialize multiple times, potentially corrupting the state of the pool.

threats.title: Liquidity manipulation
threats.approach: An attacker could create a malicious contract that mints liquidity in a way that causes the global liquidity to be inconsistent with the sum of individual positions, leading to potential loss of funds.

threats.title: Tick overflow
threats.target: Invariant: Per-tick gross liquidity never exceeds maxLiquidityPerTick
threats.approach: An attacker could manipulate the minting process to exceed the maxLiquidityPerTick by creating a large number of positions in a single transaction, causing the tick to overflow.

threats.title: Fee accrual exploitation
threats.approach: An attacker could perform a series of swaps that exploit the fee calculation logic, leading to an incorrect accrual of protocol fees that benefits the attacker.

threats.title: Oracle manipulation
threats.approach: An attacker could manipulate the observations written to the oracle by flooding the pool with transactions, causing incorrect price data to be recorded and affecting future swaps.

threats.title: Reentrancy during fee collection
threats.target: Invariant: Position tokensOwed can be collected only up to the owed amount
threats.approach: An attacker could re-enter the collect function during the fee collection process to withdraw more tokens than owed, draining the pool's assets.

threats.title: Delegatecall bypass
threats.target: Invariant: The delegatecall guard blocks delegate calls
threats.approach: An attacker could find a way to bypass the noDelegateCall guard, allowing them to execute malicious code that alters the state of the pool.

threats.title: Observation cardinality overflow
threats.target: Invariant: Oracle observationCardinality never exceeds observationCardinalityNext
threats.approach: An attacker could flood the pool with transactions that increase the observation cardinality beyond the set limit, leading to potential denial of service or incorrect oracle data.

threats.title: Incorrect fee protocol setting
threats.target: Invariant: Protocol fees are a fraction of swap fees
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the setFeeProtocol function to set an incorrect fee fraction, leading to improper distribution of fees and potential loss of funds for liquidity providers.

data.summary: Almost every transaction against this contract has to wait for the one before it. 5 slots are shared by every caller: slot0, liquidity, feeGrowthGlobal0X128 and feeGrowthGlobal1X128, and others. Any two transactions that touch one of them serialise. increaseObservationCardinalityNext(), initialize(), mint(), collect(), burn(), swap(), flash(), setFeeProtocol() and collectProtocol() cannot run alongside each other. 2 view functions were excluded: they send no transactions and never contend.
data.headline: 0% of concurrent transaction pairs run without contention. 0 of 9 entrypoints stay parallel.

hotspots.impact: One slot for every caller. increaseObservationCardinalityNext, initialize, mint, collect, burn, swap, flash, setFeeProtocol and collectProtocol write it, so those calls always execute one after another.
One slot for every caller. mint, burn and swap write it and flash read it, so those calls always execute one after another.
One slot for every caller. swap and flash write it and mint and burn read it, so those calls always execute one after another.
